correctness.rationale: For each scale, strict positive definiteness yields a unique constant-augmented interpolant, and the constant part is exactly reproduced. Decomposition by adjacent-data steps makes the induced total-variation norm precisely the maximum of finitely many single-step response variations. The Gram matrix tends to identity; its constrained solution tends uniformly on normalized data to the mean baseline and centered coefficients. A Voronoi-cell decomposition makes each peaked translate contribute one variation unit at an endpoint and two in the interior; all off-cell contributions vanish by monotone tail decay. On a step at position j the limiting gain equals 4j(n-j)/n-1, whose discrete maximum is the stated factor. Uniformity follows by a Neumann-series bound and establishes the error order. Continuous variation, not sampled output differences, is the proved quantity; the standalone checker is corroborative.

originality.rationale: Platte and Driscoll analyze Gaussian RBF interpolation through transformed polynomials, potential theory, Lebesgue constants and stable evaluation, without the present constant-augmented variation seminorm. Yarotsky derives interpolation-error formulas and analytic-function convergence for the unaugmented Gaussian span, which do not imply a sharp node-data BV operator norm in the increasingly peaked scale. Related published mathematical results concern Gaussian lattice RKHS norms, kernel-conditioning thresholds, and finite-site stability, not this kernel-universal limiting BV coefficient. No published stronger/equivalent result was identified in the available material. This is a qualified historical-priority conclusion, not proof of uniqueness.
residual_risks: The full historical literature on ordinary kriging and constant-augmented interpolation is extensive; an unindexed specialized variation-norm theorem could cover this factor.

value.rationale: The natural question is the stability of constant-reproducing narrow radial-kernel interpolation on bounded-variation sampled data. The precise answer is not given by Gaussian Gram conditioning, smooth-target convergence, or uniform-norm Lebesgue constants. The theorem computes the exact asymptotic seminorm for every fixed n, every irregular 1D grid, and a broad class of strictly positive definite monotone kernels; it identifies the central jump extremizer and linear-in-n growth, including a quantitative rate from profile tails. This gives a mathematically motivated sharp endpoint stability law, not an arbitrary data slice or mere finite calculation.
